newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drug chief asks for Caribbean cooperation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drug chief asks for Caribbean cooperation.

text.p: The top U.S. anti-drug official said on Tuesday there was no evidence to suggest that Cuban officials were involved in drug trafficking, as some Cuban-American leaders and U.S. lawmakers have suggested.

"I don't believe Cuba right now is a major factor in drug smuggling into the United States -- period," retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey told more than 200 working level diplomats and law enforcement experts gathered in Key West for three days of talks on drug fighting.

Last summer, the Cuban government angrily rejected U.S. press reports that drug traffickers arrested in the United States told U.S. agents they had smuggled drugs through Havana with the approval of President Fidel Castro.

This winter, the U.S. government praised Cuba's government for sending four officials to Miami to testify about a cocaine seizure on a freighter off Cuba's coast. At the same time, Cuban-American U.S. Congressman Lincoln Diaz-Balart issued a statement alleging a "cover up of Castro's participation in narco-trafficking."

Army spokesman Capt. Mike Park said representatives of 47 Caribbean basin nations attended the three-day session. Cuban officials were not among them, despite what Park said was a desperate effort to get them involved.
McCaffrey, one of the top generals in the 1991 Persian Gulf War, took charge of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy in February 1996.
During his tenure, some Caribbean countries, notably Jamaica, have criticised the United States for pressuring them to allow U.S. drug agents into their territories.
McCaffrey said U.S.-Caribbean cooperation was improving nonetheless. "This year -- compared to last year -- the finger-pointing's gone down 90 percent," he said.

He said stopping narcotics trafficking in the Caribbean would not be easy because of the billions of dollars of drug money coursing through the region, located strategically between U.S. drug consumers and South American drug producers.
McCaffrey also said southern Florida remained a major transit point for drugs and that more money should be dedicated to interdiction efforts in the region.

"Florida is the crossroads of the Caribbean," he said. "Thank God we've got headquarters South Comm in Miami now," he said, referring to the headquarters of the U.S. Southern Command, which is moving to south Florida from Panama.
